query: In conventional alloys, loss of toughness has long been associated with grain-boundary segregation and brittle grain-boundary precipitation. By contrast, compositionally complex high-entropy alloys can suppress rapid grain coarsening and deleterious intermetallic formation and have shown favorable strength–ductility combinations and resistance to high-temperature softening and low-temperature embrittlement. These findings do not establish what governs possible toughness degradation in an initially single-phase high-entropy alloy. Under the constraint of retaining a compositionally complex alloy suitable for demanding engineering service, what testable mechanistic hypothesis explains whether and why brittle behavior emerges? Specify a controlled comparison that would distinguish the hypothesis from conventional-alloy expectations, predicted observations relative to the initial baseline, its service and loading boundaries, supporting prior evidence, and a decisive falsification outcome.

generation.hypothesis: In an initially single-phase, compositionally complex fcc high-entropy alloy, brittle behavior emerges primarily via stress-assisted formation of chemically short-range-ordered grain-boundary complexions (nanometer-thick ordered/disordered interfacial layers without second-phase precipitation). Under intermediate temperatures where vacancies are mobile, prior or concurrent plastic deformation biases multicomponent diffusion (via vacancy wind) and local bond-preference at grain boundaries, producing SRO-rich complexions that lower boundary cohesive strength and reduce dislocation-absorption capacity. This drives a transition toward intergranular, quasi-brittle fracture and a substantial (order tens of percent) reduction in fracture toughness relative to the annealed baseline, even though classical precipitates and strong single-solute segregation are absent.
generation.material_initial_state: Single-phase fcc compositionally complex alloy (e.g., Co–Cr–Fe–Mn–Ni family), homogenized/solutionized to a random solid solution; equiaxed grains 10–50 μm; low interstitial/impurity content (O, S, C, N minimized); no detectable second phases or grain-boundary precipitates; uniform texture.
generation.intervention: Stress-assisted thermomechanical conditioning to promote interfacial SRO complexions: apply 2–5% tensile pre-strain at T ≈ 0.3–0.4 Tm under inert atmosphere, then hold under constant load at the same temperature for 1–4 h, followed by inert cooling. Controlled comparators: (i) identical thermal exposure without applied stress (no pre-strain, free-standing aging), and (ii) room-temperature pre-strain (2–5%) with no thermal hold.
generation.conditions: Characterize and fracture-test in inert environment (vacuum/Ar). Fracture tests at room temperature and at service-relevant temperatures within 0.3–0.5 Tm at quasi-static rates (10^-4–10^-3 s^-1). Microstructure probed by atom probe tomography (APT) across grain boundaries, HAADF-STEM of boundary structure, and diffraction/diffuse scattering to quantify SRO. Ensure no intermetallic precipitation by verifying single-phase diffraction and absence of second-phase contrast.
generation.structural_mediator: Stress-stabilized grain-boundary ordered complexion: a nanometer-scale interfacial layer exhibiting chemical short-range order and multicomponent compositional modulations but lacking discrete second-phase precipitates; concomitant reduction in grain-boundary dislocation sink efficiency.
generation.mechanism: Plastic straining at intermediate temperature generates vacancies and fluxes them toward grain boundaries under applied stress. Correlated, multicomponent diffusion driven by vacancy wind and local bond-preference forms SRO-enriched boundary complexions. These complexions lower grain-boundary cohesive energy and hinder dislocation absorption/transmission, elevating local stress concentrations and promoting intergranular crack nucleation and propagation. The effect is strongest within a temperature–strain-rate window where diffusion is active during or shortly after deformation but bulk precipitation remains suppressed.
generation.predicted_outcome: Relative to the annealed baseline: (a) the stress-aged HEA exhibits a substantial (order tens of percent; alloy-dependent) decrease in J_IC or K_Jc and Charpy impact energy; fracture surfaces shift from predominantly ductile, transgranular dimples to mixed or intergranular facets; EBSD/SEM shows boundary-linked crack paths. (b) APT across grain boundaries reveals multicomponent, nanoscale enrichment–depletion patterns consistent with SRO (non-monotonic, no single-element dominant segregation) and no discrete intermetallics; HAADF-STEM shows nm-thick ordered/disordered interfacial layers; diffuse scattering indicates increased SRO signatures. (c) The thermally aged (no-stress) HEA shows minimal toughness degradation and lacks pronounced SRO complexions at boundaries. (d) The effect exhibits a temperature/strain-rate window: weaker at low T (insufficient diffusion) and at higher T where SRO dissolves or boundaries relax; enhanced under faster loading that limits dislocation accommodation once complexions form.
generation.baseline: Annealed single-phase fcc HEA with random solid solution and clean grain boundaries displays high fracture toughness for its strength, ductile transgranular dimpled fracture, substantial work hardening, and no detectable grain-boundary precipitates or strong single-solute segregation.
generation.boundary: Most pronounced for intermediate homologous temperatures (≈0.3–0.5 Tm) and quasi-static to moderate strain rates where vacancy-mediated diffusion and SRO kinetics are active without triggering bulk intermetallic formation. Diminished at cryogenic/low temperatures (diffusion-limited), at very high temperatures (SRO/complexions destabilize or creep relaxes stresses), in environments containing hydrogen (additional mechanisms confound) or with significant impurity segregation (classical embrittlement pathways dominate). Alloy chemistries engineered for low SRO propensity or enhanced boundary dislocation sink capacity are expected to mitigate the effect.
generation.uncertainty: The exact magnitude of toughness decrease, the precise temperature–time–strain window, and the specific compositional signatures of SRO complexions are alloy-dependent and not yet quantified here. Subtle impurity effects or undetected nanoscale precipitates could confound interpretation if not rigorously excluded. The role of stacking-fault energy and texture in mediating dislocation–boundary interactions may modulate the severity.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare four HEA groups from the same heat: (G0) baseline annealed; (G1) stress-aged (2–5% pre-strain at 0.3–0.4 Tm, then 1–4 h hold under load); (G2) thermally aged without stress for the same time–temperature profile; (G3) room-temperature pre-strain (2–5%) with no thermal hold. Include a conventional alloy control (e.g., Ni- or Fe-base solid solution) processed analogously. After treatments, measure fracture toughness (J_IC or K_Jc) and Charpy energy at RT and service T; perform fractography (fraction intergranular), EBSD crack-path mapping, APT line scans/maps across grain boundaries, HAADF-STEM of boundary structure, and diffuse scattering/SRO quantification. Optionally, perform micro-cantilever grain-boundary fracture tests to extract boundary cohesive strength.
measurements: J_IC or K_Jc at RT and service-relevant T
APT composition profiles/maps across grain boundaries (multicomponent modulations vs single-solute segregation)
HAADF-STEM imaging of grain-boundary complexions (nm-thick ordered layers)
Diffuse scattering/SRO parameters pre- and post-treatment
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: The hypothesis is falsified if the HEA stress-aged group (G1) does not show a larger toughness decrease and higher intergranular fracture fraction than either G2 or G3, and if APT/STEM/diffuse scattering reveal no increase in SRO or ordered complexion signatures at grain boundaries relative to G0–G3; or if equivalent embrittlement occurs in G2 (aging without stress) accompanied by classical monotonic single-element segregation or grain-boundary precipitates, indicating conventional segregation/precipitation as the governing mechanism.
